findings.statement: NVIDIA's data‑center platforms integrate compute, system, networking, and software elements that customers can deploy as a service or on‑premises.
NVIDIA offers system‑level data‑center solutions under the DGX platform.
NVIDIA's current markets are the United States and Europe.
Supply lead times and eligibility for exact product configurations and destinations are identified as capacity constraints.
Cloud service providers evaluate NVIDIA offerings based on feasible data‑center capacity, grid and power access, cooling, networking, and delivery lead times, which can limit market entry.
The internal company profile does not specify any planned NVIDIA product or service for new market entry.
The brief does not assert that NVIDIA has approved a new entry, expansion, launch, or investment, indicating a gap in internal decision history.

Broadcom provides AI accelerators—including custom AI accelerators, XPUs and TPUs—and AI‑focused data‑center networking products such as Tomahawk 6, Tomahawk Ultra Ethernet switches, Jericho4 fabric switches, 400G PCIe Gen5 Ethernet NICs, and the VeloRAIN AI networking solution, all designed to support large‑scale AI workloads.

Broadcom delivers AI‑related hardware and software through a subscription model for VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF 9.0), which includes Private AI services at no extra purchase, and through a royalty‑free internal‑use software license for its AI‑related SaaS offerings, both applied in Europe and the United States.

For cloud service providers, Broadcom bundles custom AI accelerators with its Ethernet, PCIe and optical connectivity solutions into complete rack systems, and also bundles AI services (GPU monitoring, model store, runtime, etc.) within the VMware Cloud Foundation subscription, providing a unified hardware‑software‑support package.

Broadcom announced the AI‑native version of VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0, with Private AI services included in the subscription and expected to be generally available in Q1 FY26, targeting enterprises and cloud service providers in Europe, the United States and other regions.

On 13 Oct 2025 Broadcom and OpenAI announced a strategic collaboration to develop and deploy 10 GW of custom AI accelerators, with racks built using Broadcom’s Ethernet, PCIe and optical connectivity solutions, aimed at global AI data‑center deployments.

findings.statement: At the 2025 Open Compute Project Global Summit (13‑16 Oct 2025), Broadcom showcased its AI networking portfolio—including Tomahawk 6, Tomahawk Ultra Ethernet switches, Jericho4 fabric switches, and 400G PCIe Gen5 Ethernet NICs—targeted at AI‑intensive data centers in Europe, the United States and other markets.

Broadcom offers AI‑focused data‑center networking products: the Tomahawk 6 switch (shipping June 2025) and the Tomahawk Ultra networking processor (launched July 2025). Both are designed to interconnect AI compute chips at rack‑scale and are positioned as alternatives to Nvidia’s NVLink Switch.

In June 2025 Broadcom began shipping the Tomahawk 6 networking switch, targeting large AI data‑center deployments. The launch was announced for the AI infrastructure market and is available to customers in Europe and the United States.

In July 2025 Broadcom launched the Tomahawk Ultra networking processor, marketed as an AI‑scale interconnect that can link up to four times more chips using an enhanced Ethernet‑based protocol. The product is aimed at AI‑intensive data‑center customers in Europe and the United States.

On April 14 2026 Broadcom extended its partnership with Meta to co‑develop a 2‑nanometer AI compute accelerator built on Broadcom’s XPU platform, with the deal covering hardware design and advanced Ethernet technologies for Meta’s next‑generation AI data centers.

Intel Corp: Intel offers a portfolio of AI accelerators for data‑center workloads, including Habana Labs’ Gaudi training processor family, Intel Xeon Scalable processors with built‑in AI acceleration, Intel Data Center GPU Max Series, and Intel Data Center Flex Series GPUs.

Intel Corp: At Mobile World Congress 2024 (Feb 2024), Intel announced the future Intel® Xeon® processor with built‑in AI acceleration (code‑named Granite Rapids‑D), the Xeon® processor for 5G core (code‑named Sierra Forest), and a new modular Edge Platform for AI workloads, targeting data‑center and edge customers in Europe and the United States.

Intel Corp: In June 2026, Intel unveiled three next‑generation AI processors at Hot Chips 2026 – Diamond Rapids for large‑scale enterprise AI, Crescent Island for data‑center AI inference, and Wildcat Lake for laptops and edge devices – aimed at enterprise data‑center and edge markets worldwide.

Intel Corp: Intel packages its AI offerings for cloud providers as a combined stack of hardware (Xeon CPUs, Gaudi accelerators, Data Center GPU Max/Flex GPUs) plus software tools (oneAPI, OpenVINO, Intel Developer Cloud) and ecosystem support, enabling customers to select the optimal mix for training, inference, or hybrid AI workloads.

Intel Corp: Intel’s pricing model mixes per‑unit sales for hardware accelerators (Xeon, Gaudi, GPUs) with subscription‑based pricing for AI software bundles; the Software Advantage Program lists subscription prices such as US$45.00 for Canvid and US$72.00 for Capture One Pro.

findings.statement: Intel Corp: The Intel® AI Software Bundle includes subscription‑based plans with listed prices: Canvid – US$45.00, Capture One Pro – US$72.00, Luminar Neo – US$35.85, VCam.ai – US$18.00, and Render FX – US$99.99 (prices shown as ARV per subscription, interpreted as per‑seat monthly list price).
Intel Corp: Intel’s Software Advantage Program lists XSplit Premium Suite as a subscription‑based AI software with a price of US$60.00 per seat per month.

Presence in the target markets: compared with NVIDIA Corporation, Broadcom is comparable. Broadcom supplies AI accelerators and networking hardware to cloud service providers in Europe and the United States through its subscription‑based VMware Cloud Foundation offering.

Presence in the target markets: compared with NVIDIA Corporation, Intel Corp is comparable. Intel provides AI accelerators such as Habana Gaudi, Xeon CPUs with AI extensions, and Data Center GPUs to cloud service providers and enterprises in Europe and the United States, as described in its product portfolio.

Offering and localisation for those markets: compared with NVIDIA Corporation, Broadcom is comparable. Broadcom’s AI portfolio in Europe and the United States includes custom XPU/TPU accelerators, Tomahawk 6 and Ultra Ethernet switches, Jericho4 fabric switches, and 400 G PCIe Gen5 NICs, all integrated with VMware Cloud Foundation for localized deployment.

Offering and localisation for those markets: compared with NVIDIA Corporation, Intel Corp is comparable. Intel’s AI offering for Europe and the United States comprises Habana Gaudi training processors, Xeon Scalable CPUs with built‑in AI acceleration, and Data Center GPU Max/Flex GPUs, complemented by oneAPI, OpenVINO and the Intel Developer Cloud.

Pricing and packaging in those markets: compared with NVIDIA Corporation, Broadcom is different approach. Broadcom delivers its AI solutions through a subscription model for VMware Cloud Foundation and a royalty‑free internal‑use software license, rather than per‑unit hardware sales.

Pricing and packaging in those markets: compared with NVIDIA Corporation, Intel Corp is different approach. Intel combines per‑unit sales for its AI hardware (Xeon, Gaudi, GPUs) with subscription‑based AI software bundles, creating a mixed pricing structure.

Target customers and positioning: compared with NVIDIA Corporation, Broadcom is comparable. Broadcom targets cloud service providers in Europe and the United States, bundling hardware and AI services to compete directly with NVIDIA’s data‑center customers.

Target customers and positioning: compared with NVIDIA Corporation, Intel Corp is comparable. Intel addresses cloud service providers, enterprise data‑centers, and edge deployments, positioning its portfolio as a flexible alternative to GPU‑centric solutions.

Partnerships and distribution: compared with NVIDIA Corporation, Broadcom is comparable. Broadcom has announced strategic collaborations with OpenAI and Meta to develop custom AI accelerators and integrates its hardware through VMware’s distribution channel.

Recent changes: compared with NVIDIA Corporation, Broadcom is comparable. In the past 24 months Broadcom launched the AI‑native VMware Cloud Foundation 9.0, Tomahawk 6 and Ultra switches, 400 G PCIe Gen5 NICs, and announced collaborations to deploy custom AI accelerators.

Recent changes: compared with NVIDIA Corporation, Intel Corp is comparable. Intel announced the Granite Rapids‑D Xeon processor, Diamond Rapids, Crescent Island, Wildcat Lake AI processors, and a modular Edge Platform, targeting data‑center and edge markets worldwide.

The Latin America cloud computing market is projected to grow from $62.95 billion in 2025 to $125.46 billion by 2030, representing a 14.8% CAGR, indicating strong demand growth for the infrastructure that underpins AI computing platforms targeting cloud service providers and AI developers.
Indonesia has launched a telco‑led sovereign AI platform serving 270 million users, demonstrating strong demand and ecosystem support for AI computing platforms in the Indonesian market.

The United States has expanded export controls, adding 140 companies to the Entity List, broadening the Foreign Direct Product Rule (FDPR), and restricting technologies like high‑bandwidth memory, which directly impacts AI compute services and semiconductor exports.

Key AI and semiconductor value‑chain chokepoints are controlled by the Netherlands, Germany, South Korea, Japan, and Taiwan, giving these countries the ability to impose their own export controls that affect AI compute platform sales.
Microsoft launched new Azure datacenter regions in Malaysia and Indonesia in 2025, indicating expanding cloud infrastructure that supports AI computing platform adoption in these markets.
Microsoft plans to open new Azure datacenter regions in India and Taiwan in 2026, demonstrating continued investment in AI infrastructure for these high‑growth Asian markets.
Microsoft intends to deliver a second Azure datacenter region in Malaysia (Southeast Asia 3), further increasing AI‑ready cloud capacity in the region.
Indonesia delivered a telco‑led sovereign AI platform for 270 million users, demonstrating strong demand growth and ecosystem support for AI computing platforms in that market.
